strategy: Run the cartservice pod kill first to expose the widest, highest-risk user impact and measure recovery; then run a lower-than-200-user frontend load spike to test capacity without repeating the known guard breach. Together, the experiments probe shopper-visible errors and recovery, plus resource pressure and slowdown, while using different experiment types and targets.

spec.reason: Ranked first because cartservice is a single replica, a shared dependency of checkoutservice and frontend, and has reach across all five flows. Prior 30-second cartservice pod-kill runs showed errors across all flows and recovery around 22–31 seconds, making this a direct test of both the shopper-visible error blast radius and recovery.
spec.hypothesis: With the only cartservice pod terminated, shoppers will see errors across the shop until Kubernetes replaces it; all flows depend on cartservice directly or through checkout. The fault should complete and recovery should take tens of seconds.

experiments.learning_goal: Measure the live shopper impact and recovery time when the single cartservice replica is killed.

spec.reason: Frontend is a single-replica entrypoint with 200m CPU and 128Mi memory limits, so load is visible across every user flow. A previous 150-user, 30-second-ramp run completed with p95 around 1094 ms, while 200 users has previously breached the 1500 ms guard; 150 users provides visible slowdown while staying below that observed breach point.
spec.hypothesis: The increased load will put resource pressure on the single frontend and slow all flows substantially, but should complete without breaching the p95 guard or causing errors at this intensity.

experiments.learning_goal: Check whether the frontend sustains a shopper-visible, all-flow slowdown at 150 concurrent users without triggering the safety guard.

skipped_ideas.idea: network_delay on productcatalogservice at 300 ms for 60 seconds
skipped_ideas.why_not: Prior evidence shows that even 100 ms added latency makes pages about 700 ms slower; the higher intensity risks simply tripping the slowdown guard and teaches less than the controlled load test.

Prior runs at this intensity caused broad shopper-visible errors and guard aborts. The cartservice pod kill already probes broad outage impact and recovery, so this would add destructive risk without enough distinct learning.
It would expose checkout errors, but its impact is limited to the checkout path and overlaps the error-class learning from the broader cartservice outage.
